source.title: VLA-RL: Towards Masterful and General Robotic Manipulation with Scalable Reinforcement Learning
source.authors: Guanxing Lu; Wenkai Guo; Chubin Zhang; Yuheng Zhou; Haonan Jiang; Zifeng Gao; Yansong Tang; Ziwei Wang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies the idea of scaling to robotic manipulation and reports success-rate results across RL training checkpoints, but does not test language-model pretraining loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure held-out cross-entropy, sweep model parameters, training tokens or compute, fit power laws, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its own scaling-related result is success rate across RL training steps on LIBERO. Other benchmark comparisons and ablations are not results about scaling-law behavior.
record.test_reason: This is a robotics RL fine-tuning method paper. Its only 'scaling' result is the success rate of one OpenVLA-7B policy across RL training checkpoints. It does not vary parameters, tokens or pretraining compute. It measures no held-out loss, fits no power law and makes no prediction from scale or loss. 'Inference scaling laws' is cited only as an analogy (Snell et al.). The curve reports the authors' own method's performance over training, so it does not test V6 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that VLA-RL improves OpenVLA-7B by 4.5% on LIBERO and matches π0-FAST. They also say performance scaling with 'test-time optimization' (actually RL training steps) suggests a principle analogous to inference scaling laws. They present this as preliminary, not as a fitted law.
record.recipe_differences: Measures robotic task success across RL training steps rather than language-model held-out loss across model size, tokens or compute; it does not fit a power law or optimize a parameter/token split.

fits_no_version.finding: Robotic task success of RL-fine-tuned OpenVLA-7B on LIBERO rises over 10k RL training steps. Average goes from about 76.3 to 81.0 against SFT 76.5, with a small dip mid-run. The authors call this an 'early spark of inference scaling laws'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream success of a fixed-size VLA policy improves with the number of online RL fine-tuning steps (RL post-training compute), with no fitted functional form.

record.problems: The scaling-related result is reported for OpenVLA-7B on simulated LIBERO tasks and is described qualitatively in the text; the study does not establish a fitted or predictive scaling law, and RL training steps are not a sweep over model size, tokens or compute.
record.rows_left_out: No other scaling-related results were reported. Benchmark comparisons and ablations concern method performance or implementation choices, not the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining-loss measurements versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no fitted law and no extrapolation.
All: no power-law fit in robotics or RL fine-tuning; only a short success-rate curve with five checkpoints.
All: no variation in model scale or pretraining loss; downstream success is tracked only over RL steps of one model.
All: no exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label is dropped. Improvement over RL fine-tuning steps of one 7B model is neither scale nor pretraining loss, and it is the method's own performance curve. The ablations (Table 2) and benchmark comparisons (Table 1) are method results and correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on smaller runs predict substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of architecture depth, width and other details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes.
The study reports downstream robotic task success over RL training steps, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss, model size, or a fitted scaling relation.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: OpenVLA-7B
rows.stage_stated: RL fine-tuned from an SFT checkpoint
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated task success rates at intervals during RL training; evaluations were every 2500 training steps.

conditions.value: complete suite; average task success rates

rows.measure: Average task success rate across RL training steps
rows.value: figure only; text states evaluation success rates on all four task suites consistently improved with training
rows.note: The paper describes this as test-time scaling, but the plotted progression is along RL training steps. The text gives an aggregate statement for all four suites; no numeric curve values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The row measures the success of the authors' own RL fine-tuning method across training steps for a single fixed-size model. That is not downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss (V6), and no power-law form is fitted (V5). 'Figure only' is inaccurate: Fig. 1 and Fig. 4 print point values. LIBERO average is about 76.3 → 77.6 → 79.0 → 78.9 → 81.0 against SFT 76.5. Spatial ends at 90.2 vs SFT 84.7, Long at 59.8 vs SFT 53.7. The curves are not strictly monotone (e.g. average 79.0 → 78.9), despite the authors calling them 'consistently improved'.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: OpenVLA-7B on the four LIBERO task suites across RL training checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: The authors report consistently improving evaluation success rates across training steps; this is evidence of downstream task performance improving in the tested robotic setting (r1).
